summary:
Ghost Fleet is an interactive 3D documentary about 15 machines NASA left behind: on the Moon (Surveyor, Apollo 11's Eagle, ALSEP, the lunar rovers), on Mars (Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity) and in deep space (Pioneer 10 & 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler). Built for school-age and casual space fans, each machine tells its own story in first person, from launch on Earth to where it rests today.

Visitors explore a 3D scene with Earth, the Moon and Mars, then pick a machine. Its mission plays as a short 3D film in seven phases: Launch, Cruise, Arrival, Mission, Discovery, Legacy and Today. Rockets lift off and stage, landers descend through Mars' atmosphere, rovers drive, Ingenuity flies, and seismographs record marsquakes. A different natural-sounding voice narrates each machine, with optional subtitles. Each story ends with a three-question quiz, and scores are saved across visits.

Every fact traces back to NASA sources (NSSDCA and NASA Science mission pages). Most spacecraft are official models from NASA's 3D library. We aim to show how each machine's engineering led to real discoveries, so young explorers feel a personal connection to these silent robots and the science they made possible.

Built with React, three.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel.
details:
Ghost Fleet is an interactive 3D documentary about the hardware NASA has left behind across the solar system. It covers 15 machines:

- On the Moon: Surveyor, Apollo 11's Eagle, the ALSEP science stations and the Lunar Roving Vehicles.

- On Mars: Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity.

- In deep space: Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn and Kepler.

Visitors start in a 3D scene they can orbit and zoom. Earth shows city lights on its night side, and the Moon and Mars have NASA spacecraft circling them. From there they open a Moon or Mars globe with markers at the real landing coordinates, or a map of deep space.

Choosing a machine starts its story. It plays as a short 3D film, narrated in first person by the machine itself, in seven phases: Launch, Cruise, Arrival, Mission, Discovery, Legacy and Today. The viewer sees:

- the rocket lift off and drop its stages;

- the spacecraft cross space with a day counter;

- landers plunge through the Martian atmosphere with heat shields, parachutes, airbags or a sky crane;

- rovers drive and leave tracks, and Ingenuity fly;

- a seismograph record marsquakes;

- a cutaway of the inside of Mars;

- a star dim as an exoplanet crosses it.

Each story ends where the machine rests today, often with a fading "signal lost". Then comes a three-question quiz. Scores and "ghosts found" are saved, which encourages visitors to explore every mission. A Mission File panel holds the facts, the launch rocket, the science each machine made possible, and links to its NASA source.

Benefits and intended impact

Most young people only hear about active missions. Ghost Fleet turns retired hardware into characters with a beginning, a middle and an end. Instead of reading a list of facts, learners watch how a mission actually worked and connect engineering to discovery:

- Airbags and rocker-bogie wheels made rovers possible.

- A sensitive seismometer revealed the size of Mars' core.

- A laser mirror on the Moon shows it drifts away 3.8 cm a year.

The Legacy phase shows how each mission paved the way for the next: Pioneer for Voyager, NEAR for OSIRIS-REx, Kepler for TESS and Webb. Our goal is for students to feel a personal connection to these silent explorers and to see themselves as the next generation who will build what comes after.

Tools and technologies

- Code: TypeScript and React, with three.js through React Three Fiber and Drei for real-time 3D. Built with Vite and deployed on Vercel. It runs in any modern web browser, on desktop and phones, with no install.

- 3D models: 22 official NASA 3D models, including Saturn V, the Apollo Lunar Module, Viking, Perseverance, Ingenuity, InSight, LRO, MRO, Voyager, OSIRIS-REx, TESS, the James Webb Space Telescope, the ISS, Hubble, the Deep Space Network antenna and the Vehicle Assembly Building. We built simplified models for hardware with no available model: the lunar rover, Surveyor, ALSEP, Sojourner, and the Atlas, Delta and Titan rockets.

- Maps: NASA's CGI Moon Kit lunar map, and Solar System Scope textures for Earth, Mars, Jupiter and the Milky Way.

- Narration: pre-generated with neural text-to-speech, plus word timings that drive the synced subtitles.

- Data: NSSDCA and NASA Science mission pages.

Creativity

Each machine speaks as itself, with its own distinct voice, so a 1960s lander sounds different from a 2021 helicopter. The story is told through animated 3D scenes rather than text: viewers watch a rocket launch, a Mars landing or a moonquake instead of reading about it. Small touches make it feel real: wheel tracks on the ground, Moon dust that flies in clean arcs because there is no air, a live light curve that dips as a planet passes its star. Each film ends with the machine's last signal fading out.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy first: every date, number and landing coordinate was checked against NASA records, and errors we found were corrected.

- Audience: language written for roughly ages 10 and up, short scenes, and a quiz for every mission.

- Accessibility: subtitles that can be turned on or off, mutable narration, keyboard controls, a mobile layout, and a pause that freezes the scene so viewers can look around at their own pace.

- Performance: compressed models and scenes that load on demand, so the site runs smoothly in a browser.

- Attribution: licenses and credits for every model, texture and source are listed inside the app.
